1.title: Troubleshooting Kubernetes
1.text: Welcome to Module 9: Troubleshooting Kubernetes. This module is in the Container Orchestration domain, and it covers the topic called Troubleshooting. By the end you will be able to do four things. Use a symptom-to-layer method and the core kube control tools. Read Pod states such as Pending, Image Pull Back Off, Crash Loop Back Off and O O M Killed. Diagnose a Service with no endpoints, D N S failures and a Not Ready node. And recognize quota and R B A C denials, and find component logs.

1.title: Case Check-In: Harbor Books Has a Bad Morning
1.text: At Harbor Books, a new orders Pod stays Pending, and nobody knows why. The storefront cannot reach catalog, although the catalog Pods are running. One worker node reports Not Ready, and a developer's request is rejected as Forbidden. In this module you find which layer is at fault.

1.title: A Symptom-to-Layer Method
1.text: Good troubleshooting starts with triage. Is the problem in the Pod, in its controller or in the Service? Read the symptom, then name the layer. The layers are scheduling, container, network, storage, node and access. The diagram links each symptom to its layer. Pending points to scheduling. Image Pull Back Off, Crash Loop Back Off and O O M Killed point to the container. No endpoints and D N S point to the network. Then inspect that layer with describe, events and logs. Change one thing at a time, and check that the symptom is gone. Exam tip: symptom first, then the layer, then the matching command.

1.title: kubectl Tools for Troubleshooting
1.text: Six kube control commands cover most cases. Get shows the state and the restarts. Describe ends with the events, which explain why. Get events lists recent events for a namespace. Logs with the previous option shows the log of the crashed container. Exec runs a command, or opens a shell, inside a container, and debug adds an ephemeral container. And top shows C P U and memory use, when the Metrics Server is installed. Exam tip: describe says why, and logs say what the application printed.

1.title: Pod States and What They Mean
1.text: Six states to know. Pending means the Pod is accepted but not placed on a node yet, so read the events in describe. Image Pull Back Off means the image cannot be pulled, and Kubernetes retries with a growing delay. Check the image name, the registry and the image pull secret. Crash Loop Back Off means the container keeps failing and restarting, so read the previous logs and the configuration. O O M Killed means the container used more memory than its limit. Evicted means the kube let ended the Pod under node pressure. And Terminating means a deletion was issued but cannot finish, often because of finalizers and admission webhooks. Exam tip: Pending is about placement, and the Back Off states are about the container.

1.title: Pending in Detail
1.text: A Pending Pod has been accepted but not placed. Describe shows the scheduler's reason, and the reason is usually one of three. Resources: not enough C P U or memory for its requests, so free resources, lower the requests or add nodes. Placement: selectors, affinity or taints match no node, as in Module 5, or a host Port limits where it can go. Storage: a claim that cannot bind keeps the Pod from being placed, as in Module 7. The diagram shows the three branches under the Pending Pod. Exam tip: Pending, read the events first.

1.title: NotReady Nodes and Component Logs
1.text: When a node stops reporting, it shows Not Ready. The cause may be a node that is down, cut off from the network, or a dead kube let. The node controller marks the Ready condition as Unknown, and by default it evicts the Pods on that node after five minutes. Kube control get nodes and kube control describe node show the condition and the events. For logs, the control plane has the kube A P I server, the kube scheduler and the kube controller manager. Workers have the kube let and kube proxy. On systemd hosts the kube let and the runtime write to journald, so use journal control. Exam tip: Not Ready, look at the node and its kube let.

1.title: A Service With No Endpoints, and DNS Failures
1.text: When a Service does not work, walk the path of a request in order. Does the Service exist? Does its name resolve? Does it have Endpoint Slices? No endpoints points to a selector that matches no Pods, so compare it with the labels of the Pods. The Pod's container Port must match the Service's target Port. For D N S, run ns lookup from a Pod, and check that the Core D N S Pods, labeled k eight s dash app equals kube dash D N S, are running. Then look at kube proxy and any Network Policy. Exam tip: no endpoints, compare the selector with the Pod labels.

1.title: Quota and RBAC Denials
1.text: Two kinds of Forbidden, both with status four hundred and three. An R B A C denial means no role grants the action to that user or Service Account. Check with kube control auth can-i, and then the roles and bindings. A quota denial means the request would break a Resource Quota, and the message names the constraint. Check with kube control describe quota in the namespace. Both come from the control plane, and they are policy answers, so the cluster is healthy. With quotas on for C P U or memory, a Pod must state requests or limits, or it is rejected. Exam tip: a four hundred and three is a policy answer, not a broken cluster.

1.title: What the Exam Asks: Troubleshooting
1.text: Six pairs to keep apart. Pending or Image Pull Back Off: not placed yet, or placed but the image cannot be pulled. Crash Loop Back Off or O O M Killed: the container keeps failing, or it hit its memory limit. Describe or logs: events and state, or what the application printed, with the previous option for a crashed container. No endpoints: the selector and the Pod labels do not match. Not Ready: the node or its kube let, and Pods are evicted after five minutes by default. And Forbidden: R B A C or a quota, not a cluster fault. Exam tip: name the layer before you pick a command.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: To recap. The method is symptom, layer, inspect, fix one thing, verify. The tools are get, describe, events, logs with the previous option, exec, debug and top. For Pod states, Pending is placement, Image Pull Back Off is the image, Crash Loop Back Off is the container, and O O M Killed is the memory limit. Pending comes from resources, placement rules or a claim that cannot bind. A Not Ready node means a dead kube let or network, so read the component logs. No endpoints is a selector mismatch, and a four hundred and three is R B A C or a quota. Now five practice questions.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A container keeps crashing and restarting. Which command shows the log of its previous, crashed instance? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. The previous option of the logs command shows the log of the container that crashed. Top shows resource use, and events and describe show state changes but not the application's output.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A new Harbor Books orders Pod stays Pending, and describe shows that no node has enough free C P U for its requests. Which actions can fix this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Pending means the Pod is not placed, and here the reason is C P U requests that no node can satisfy. Lowering requests, freeing resources or adding nodes addresses that. A Service, a control plane kube let and a memory limit have nothing to do with it.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A worker node shows Not Ready in kube control get nodes. Which cause is likely? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A node that stops reporting, because it is down, cut off or its kube let died, gets the Ready condition Unknown and shows Not Ready. Labels, replica counts and Service selectors do not make a node Not Ready.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. The Harbor Books storefront cannot reach catalog through its Service. The Endpoint Slices of the Service list no addresses, yet the catalog Pods are Running. What is the likely cause? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Endpoint Slices list the Pods that match the Service selector, so an empty list with running Pods points to a selector or label mismatch. A D N S failure would break name resolution, not the endpoint list, and Cluster I P Services do have Endpoint Slices.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A request to create more Pods in a namespace is rejected with four hundred and three Forbidden, and the message says a quota would be exceeded. Which statement is correct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A request that would violate a Resource Quota is rejected by the control plane with four hundred and three Forbidden, and a message naming the constraint. It is a policy answer, not an eviction, an R B A C denial or a proxy problem.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are the answers at a glance. Question one, B: logs with the previous option. Question two, A: lower requests, free resources or add nodes. Question three, D: a stopped kube let or a lost connection. Question four, C: the selector does not match the Pod labels. Question five, B: the Resource Quota was exceeded.
